kinds.name: A driver
steps: Look at the kernel drivers registered shortly before the crash: hardware monitoring, overclocking, RGB, anti-cheat and antivirus tools install their own, and they are the usual suspects.
Update or uninstall the most recent of them, then watch whether the crash comes back.
Update the graphics, network, storage and chipset drivers from the manufacturer rather than through a driver updater.

kinds.name: Memory, or a driver corrupting it
steps: Run the Windows Memory Diagnostic from Diagnostics, Hardware tests, Memory.
Remove any overclock or XMP/EXPO memory profile and test again at the default speed.
If memory tests clean, treat it as a driver problem: the same code is often a driver writing where it should not.

kinds.name: Storage
steps: Read Storage health first: a failing disk explains this family of codes.
Update the storage controller driver and the SSD firmware.
Check the cable or the seating of the drive, then run chkdsk on the system volume.

kinds.name: The graphics driver or card
steps: Install the current driver from the card manufacturer, removing the old one first.
Remove any GPU overclock and check the card temperature under load.
If a new driver started it, roll back to the previous version.

kinds.name: Hardware
steps: Remove every overclock and undervolt, and load the firmware defaults.
Check temperatures and cooling under load.
Update the system firmware; a processor reporting uncorrectable errors after that needs the hardware checked.

kinds.name: Power management
steps: Note whether it happens on sleep, resume or shutdown.
Update the chipset, graphics and network drivers, and the system firmware.
Turn off fast startup to see whether the crash stops.

kinds.name: Windows system files
steps: Run the System File Checker and the DISM repair from Fixes.
Read Storage health, because damaged system files often come from a failing disk.
Check whether the crash started with an update, in Update history.

kinds.name: Firmware
steps: Update the system firmware from the manufacturer.
Load the firmware defaults, then change only what is needed.

kinds.name: Started on purpose
steps: Nothing is broken: the crash was triggered deliberately, by a key combination set up for debugging, a tool, or holding the power button.

codes.meaning: A driver, or faulty memory, accessed memory it was not allowed to at that moment.
A memory pool header was found corrupted, usually by a driver.
The memory manager found its own structures damaged. Faulty memory is the first suspect.
Code running in the kernel raised an exception that nothing handled.
The NTFS file system driver hit a problem, typically damage on the disk.
An exception happened while a system service was running, often in a graphics or antivirus driver.
Memory that must always be present was referenced and was not valid: faulty memory, a driver or antivirus software.
The system registry hive is damaged.
Kernel data could not be read back from the paging file.
Kernel data could not be read from the disk into memory: a failing disk, cable or controller.
Windows lost access to the system drive during start up: a changed storage controller mode, a driver, or the disk itself.
A system thread raised an exception that nothing handled.
The processor raised a trap the kernel did not catch: unstable hardware, overheating, or a driver.
A hardware failure was signalled to the processor.
The processor reported a fatal machine check error.
A driver did not finish a power transition in time, often on sleep, resume or shutdown.
The power policy manager hit a fatal error, often around hibernation.
The firmware ACPI tables are not compatible with Windows.
A driver tried to write to read only memory.
A driver made a bad memory pool request.
Driver Verifier caught a driver breaking a rule. Verifier is turned on for this machine; turn it off with verifier /reset once the driver is known.
A driver corrupted the kernel memory pool.
A driver accessed pageable memory at a moment it was not allowed to. Network, storage and antivirus drivers are the usual cause.
The crash was started deliberately.
The system volume could not be mounted during start up.
A process Windows cannot run without stopped. Damaged system files and a failing disk are the common causes.
A critical process or thread ended, most often because the disk stopped answering.
A driver overran a buffer on its stack. Windows stopped on purpose, because that is how an attack takes control of the kernel.
Code tried to run from memory marked as not executable.
A USB driver hit a fatal error.
A processor stopped answering its clock interrupt: processor instability from overclocking, voltage or heat, or old firmware.
Kernel code or data was modified: a driver patching the kernel, or faulty memory.
A driver built on the Windows Driver Framework broke a framework rule.
The graphics kernel hit a fatal error.
The graphics driver stopped responding and could not be recovered.
The graphics driver stopped responding and was reset.
The graphics scheduler hit a fatal error.
The processor reported an uncorrectable hardware error: processor, memory, heat, voltage or overclocking.
A single bit error was found in a memory page: faulty memory.
A deferred procedure call ran too long, typically in a storage or network driver, or SSD firmware.
The kernel detected that a critical data structure was corrupted, usually by a driver.
The kernel heap was corrupted, usually by a driver.
A USB 3 controller or driver hit a fatal error.
The memory store component raised an unexpected exception, most often because of the disk or its firmware.
An exception was raised on a stack that was not valid: kernel stack corruption, typically by a driver.
The power button was held to force the crash.
A driver took too long to handle a Plug and Play operation.
A critical user mode subsystem failed, often after a damaged update or system files.
The crash was started deliberately.
